title: Primary hyperparathyroidism: reading the calcium results and planning surgery

header.contentArea: Endocrine surgery: hypercalcaemia and primary hyperparathyroidism (results released in stages)

related.why: Anatomy of the parathyroids and the recurrent laryngeal nerve at neck exploration
Hypocalcaemia and neck haematoma after thyroid and parathyroid surgery
The other endocrine surgery viva: adrenal incidentaloma and phaeochromocytoma

brief.scenario: Mrs Isla Cairncross, 58, has had two episodes of renal colic in a year and complains of thirst and constipation. Her GP found a raised calcium.
brief.task: The examiner will give you her results in stages. Interpret them and discuss her assessment and management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Calcium with PTH first. Exclude FHH, measure vitamin D, look for end-organ damage, then refer against NG132.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Using imaging to make the diagnosis, or quoting old age and bone-density rules as the NICE criteria.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "A high calcium with a PTH that is not suppressed means primary hyperparathyroidism until proven otherwise."

grid.label: Interpret calcium and PTH
grid.fail: Calls it hypercalcaemia of malignancy, or ignores the raised PTH.
grid.pass: Raised albumin-adjusted calcium on repeat with raised PTH: primary hyperparathyroidism. Low PTH points to other causes, including malignancy.
grid.high: Notes a PTH in the normal range is inappropriate when calcium is high; lists PTH-suppressed causes: malignancy (PTHrP, bone metastases), vitamin D excess, thiazides.

grid.label: Exclude FHH, check vitamin D
grid.fail: Proceeds to surgery without measuring urine calcium.
grid.pass: Measures urine calcium excretion (24-hour, or calcium:creatinine clearance ratio) to exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia; measures vitamin D.
grid.high: Explains FHH is benign and parathyroidectomy does not cure it; replaces vitamin D if low.

grid.label: End-organ assessment
grid.fail: Does not look for bone or kidney effects.
grid.pass: eGFR or creatinine, DXA of lumbar spine, distal radius and hip, and renal tract ultrasound.
grid.high: Links findings back to referral: stones, osteoporosis or fragility fracture are end-organ disease.

grid.label: Referral for surgery
grid.fail: Quotes age under 50 or bone-density thresholds as the NICE criteria, or waits for symptoms to worsen.
grid.pass: Refer to a parathyroid surgeon: symptoms of hypercalcaemia, end-organ disease, or adjusted calcium 2.85 mmol/L or above.
grid.high: Notes she meets all three; NICE also allows referral of patients without these features.

grid.label: Localisation imaging
grid.fail: Uses sestamibi or ultrasound to make or exclude the diagnosis.
grid.pass: Imaging only localises before surgery: ultrasound first, sestamibi if it would guide the approach.
grid.high: Negative or discordant scans do not cancel surgery: four-gland exploration by an experienced surgeon; ectopic adenoma to a specialist centre.

grid.label: Surgery and follow-up
grid.fail: Recommends routine intraoperative PTH monitoring, or no follow-up calcium.
grid.pass: Single adenoma on imaging: choice of focused parathyroidectomy or four-gland exploration. No intraoperative PTH monitoring at first-time surgery.
grid.high: Calcium and PTH before discharge; calcium at 3 to 6 months to confirm cure, then yearly.

grid.label: Pathology
grid.pass: Usually a single parathyroid adenoma; less often multigland hyperplasia; carcinoma rarely.
grid.high: Multigland disease suggests MEN syndromes; a very high calcium with a neck mass raises carcinoma.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Adjusted calcium 2.92 mmol/L twice, PTH 12.4 pmol/L. Interpret.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: High calcium in a woman her age, so I'd worry about bone metastases.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Nothing more. I'd list her for parathyroidectomy.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Not really, the blood tests are enough.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Age under 50, a T-score below minus 2.5, or calcium well above normal.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How do you confirm the diagnosis?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: A sestamibi scan. If it's negative, it isn't hyperparathyroidism.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: How do you know the operation worked?

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Adjusted calcium 2.92 mmol/L twice, PTH 12.4 pmol/L. Interpret.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: High calcium with raised PTH: primary hyperparathyroidism. If the PTH were low I'd look for malignancy.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Urine calcium excretion to exclude familial hypocalciuric hypercalcaemia, and vitamin D.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: eGFR, a DXA of the lumbar spine, distal radius and hip, and a renal tract ultrasound.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Yes: she has symptoms, stones, and a calcium above 2.85.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Ultrasound to localise, then sestamibi if it would guide surgery. Imaging doesn't make the diagnosis.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Ultrasound and sestamibi agree: right inferior adenoma.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: She can choose focused parathyroidectomy or four-gland exploration. NICE says no intraoperative PTH at first-time surgery.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A single adenoma; less often hyperplasia; rarely carcinoma.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Calcium 2.92 with a raised PTH is primary hyperparathyroidism. Even a PTH in the normal range would be inappropriate here. A suppressed PTH would mean malignancy, vitamin D excess or thiazides.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Urine calcium:creatinine clearance ratio is 0.024; vitamin D is 38 nmol/L.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That doesn't suggest FHH, which matters because surgery doesn't cure FHH. I'd replace her vitamin D.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: DXA shows a T-score of minus 2.7 at the distal radius.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: That's osteoporosis, so with her stones she has end-organ disease in bone and kidney.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: So does she meet NICE criteria?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: On all three counts: symptoms, end-organ disease and calcium over 2.85. NICE also lets us refer people who meet none of them.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: She'd still have surgery: four-gland exploration by an experienced parathyroid surgeon. If imaging showed an ectopic gland, I'd refer to a specialist centre.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: How will you follow her up?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Calcium and PTH before discharge, calcium at 3 to 6 months to confirm cure, then yearly.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: If all four glands were enlarged?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Multigland hyperplasia: I'd think about MEN syndromes and ask about family history.

failures.consequence: A patient with FHH has a neck exploration that cannot lower her calcium.

failures.move: Using a negative sestamibi scan to rule out the diagnosis or cancel surgery.
failures.consequence: A biochemically proven disease goes untreated and her stones and bone loss continue.

failures.move: Applying age and T-score rules instead of NG132.
failures.consequence: Symptomatic patients with end-organ disease are not referred.

failures.move: Planning routine intraoperative PTH monitoring at first-time surgery.
failures.consequence: Goes against NG132, which advises against it at first-time parathyroid surgery.

recovery.line: Under NG132 the triggers are symptoms, end-organ disease or calcium of 2.85 or above.
The diagnosis is biochemical; imaging only plans the operation.

knowledge.fact: Raised adjusted calcium with raised or unsuppressed PTH: primary hyperparathyroidism. Low PTH: look for malignancy.
Exclude FHH with urine calcium excretion; measure and replace vitamin D.
After diagnosis: eGFR, DXA (lumbar spine, distal radius, hip), renal tract ultrasound.
Refer for surgery: symptoms, end-organ disease (stones, fragility fracture, osteoporosis) or adjusted calcium 2.85 mmol/L or above.
Imaging localises only; operate even if scans are negative. No intraoperative PTH at first-time surgery.
Cure confirmed by normal calcium 3 to 6 months after surgery.

recall.think: Stones, bones and a calcium that keeps rising; FHH that surgery cannot cure.

numbers.meaning: Adjusted calcium that alone triggers surgical referral
Calcium check to confirm surgical cure

recall.trap: A negative sestamibi scan does not exclude the disease.
recall.finish: Parathyroidectomy by an experienced surgeon; no intraoperative PTH first time.

partner.opening: Mrs Cairncross has renal stones, thirst and constipation. Her albumin-adjusted calcium is 2.92 mmol/L on two occasions and her PTH is 12.4 pmol/L (reference 1.6 to 6.9). Interpret these results.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for urine calcium and vitamin D
reveals.finding: Calcium:creatinine clearance ratio 0.024 (laboratory comment: not suggestive of FHH). 25-hydroxyvitamin D 38 nmol/L.
eGFR 74. DXA: T-score minus 2.7 at the distal radius. Renal ultrasound: two small left renal calculi.
Ultrasound: 12 mm hypoechoic nodule behind the lower pole of the right thyroid lobe. Sestamibi: concordant uptake, right inferior.

push.question: What does the PTH tell you?
push.expect: Unsuppressed PTH with high calcium: primary hyperparathyroidism.

push.question: What must you exclude before surgery?
push.expect: FHH by urine calcium excretion; check vitamin D.

push.question: Does she meet NICE referral criteria?
push.expect: Yes: symptoms, end-organ disease, calcium 2.85 or above.

push.question: Would you use intraoperative PTH monitoring?
How do you know she is cured?
push.expect: Normal calcium 3 to 6 months after surgery.

curveballs.prompt: Both scans are negative. Do we still operate?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Yes: four-gland exploration by an experienced surgeon; imaging is not diagnostic.

curveballs.prompt: Her PTH comes back at the top of the normal range.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Still inappropriate for the calcium; consistent with primary hyperparathyroidism; seek specialist advice.

curveballs.prompt: She would rather not have surgery. Can we give a bisphosphonate for the calcium?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Not for the hypercalcaemia; cinacalcet can be considered if surgery is declined and calcium is high enough; bisphosphonate only for fracture risk.
